item.title: How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole?
item.description: Astrophysicist Shep Doeleman explains how capturing the first image of a black hole required a telescope the size of the world, and why the next goal is to create a movie. The post How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole? first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Ultrathin metal layer boosts spin-related signals, opening a door to ultralow-power electronics
item.description: Researchers at Kyushu University have found that an ultrathin layer of iridium manganese (IrMn) can improve two spin-related signals in a structure made of a magnetic insulator and a platinum film. By examining how spin currents are generated and absorbed, the team gained insights into how the intermediate layer improves spin transfer. The findings could inform the development of ultralow-power devices for computing and energy harvesting.

item.title: Machine learning helps track semiconductor defects under more realistic temperature conditions
item.description: All materials contain inherent defects. These are not always harmful, since they can be used to engineer and introduce certain properties into a material. However, it is crucial to understand how they function and how they affect the material's properties.

item.title: Against all expectations, researchers control the magnetic core of a single atom
item.description: Researchers at Delft University of Technology (the Netherlands) have succeeded in controlling the magnetism in the nucleus of a single atom with radio waves. This came as a surprise: until now, physicists believed that this nuclear spin could not be manipulated directly. The discovery could open up new possibilities for storing and reading quantum information. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

item.title: SPINE: A machine-learning program is on the trail of ghost particles
item.description: Neutrinos are among the most abundant particles in the universe, but they are also among the most elusive. Nearly massless, they are produced by nuclear reactions in the sun, exploding stars, particle accelerators and even the decay of radioactive elements on Earth. They interact so weakly with ordinary matter that trillions pass through each person every second without leaving a trace. Studying these ghostly particles could help answer some of the biggest questions in physics, from the nature o

item.title: Quantum sensor loop design could improve magnetic measurements for medicine and communications
item.description: Adelaide University quantum engineers have found a new way to improve some of the world's most sensitive sensors of electromagnetic fields, a breakthrough that could help advance brain imaging, medical diagnostics, communications technology and next-generation quantum devices.

item.title: New X-ray method isolates faint signals from water at material surfaces
item.description: A research team from Toyohashi University of Technology, the Institute for Molecular Science and the Institute of Science Tokyo, led by Yu Kinjo and professor Ryugo Tero of Toyohashi University of Technology, has developed a new method to investigate the state of water near material surfaces using X-rays. By combining X-ray absorption spectroscopy with data analysis, the researchers separated the weak signals of interfacial water from those of the much larger amount of surrounding water.

item.title: How the quantum vacuum perturbs atoms, could shrink black holes and may have helped form galaxies
item.description: The word "vacuum" may conjure the image of empty space. Maybe you think of a region far outside the solar system without planets, debris, gas clouds or light. According to quantum theory, however, a vacuum is never truly empty. Quantum mechanics extends the Heisenberg uncertainty principle—which states that we cannot measure the position and the velocity of an object exactly at the same time—to a vacuum. The result is that a vacuum can never be still.

item.title: Electrical signals reveal hidden magnetic information in altermagnets for first time
item.description: Researchers have experimentally demonstrated, for the first time, that it is possible to obtain from an altermagnet a spin current that can transport magnetic information. This result is supported by the theoretical model of electron transport developed by the CFM group. Altermagnets are a new class of materials that, despite not exhibiting the net magnetization characteristic of conventional magnets, can generate this type of current.

item.title: A blue laser for underwater communication and sensing
item.description: Researchers at EPFL have developed a chip-scale blue laser that combines stable light emission with rapid frequency control, opening possibilities for underwater communication, environmental sensing and quantum technologies.

item.title: Explaining the difference between brittle and ductile behavior in polymer glasses
item.description: Glasses are (mostly) brittle, metals can be ductile (plastic), and liquids flow easily. Polymers are interesting because they exhibit all three types of behavior, depending on their chemical nature, temperature, and deformation rate. If polymers are not able to crystallize, their low-temperature state is glassy, and they are hard and transparent. One example is poly(methylmethacrylate) [PMMA], which has been used as an artificial glass since the early 20th century.

item.title: When simulations fall short, this spectrometer learns for itself
item.description: An NMR spectrometer can reveal molecular structure down to the atomic level, but weak signals limit what it can see. Now, Aarhus University researchers have used AI to let the spectrometer learn the best pulse sequence directly from the sample.

item.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
item.description: More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occur

item.title: Sound-levitated particles reveal how static charge builds up
item.description: When two objects touch and then separate, they can swap tiny amounts of electric charge, even if they are made from exactly the same material. This 'triboelectric effect' is the source of everyday static electricity, but it is still poorly understood in large samples of powder, where vast numbers of particles are constantly colliding with each other.

item.title: How Spiders Spin ‘Silk Dope’ Into Nature’s Toughest Material
item.description: By probing its molecular structure, biologists are uncovering how a tangle of unstructured proteins turns into a tough, flexible thread. The post How Spiders Spin ‘Silk Dope’ Into Nature’s Toughest Material first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: Decoding the loopy physics of hula hooping with high-tech earthquake sensors
item.description: Hula hooping may be literal child's play, but as it turns out, the physics behind the gym-class staple is so complicated that scientists have spent decades trying to understand how the hula hoop defies gravity.

item.title: Identical vesicles, different behaviors: Model reveals how spontaneous asymmetry gives rise to lifelike behavior
item.description: In nonreciprocal active matter, agents act differently on each other, seemingly in violation of Newton's third law. This principle can result in various active matter traits, such as self-propulsion, molecular regulation and collective motion.

item.title: Quantum gates set speed record at 6.8 nanoseconds with over 99.98% accuracy
item.description: Researchers from Jülich, Aachen and Cologne have performed a quantum operation on a qubit in just 6.8 nanoseconds—with more than 99.98% accuracy. Such operations typically take several tens of nanoseconds in superconducting quantum computers. The paper was published in Nature Communications.

item.title: Microscopic springs transform fragile silicon into a flexible terahertz metamaterial
item.description: Researchers at the Osaka Research Institute of Industrial Science and Technology (ORIST), in collaboration with the University of Osaka and Tohoku University, have developed a flexible and stretchable silicon material whose response to terahertz waves can be mechanically tuned. By etching microscopic spiral springs into silicon, the team made the fragile material bendable and stretchable.

item.title: New converter could bridge light wavelength gap in quantum communications
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices using quantum mechanical effects, could potentially allow users to share information more securely and efficiently. Building these networks typically entails linking stationary qubits, units of quantum information encoded in trapped ions or other physical systems, using photons (particles of light) transmitted through optical fibers.

item.title: Metalens microscope switches focus with voltage, not moving optics
item.description: Just as it is difficult for a camera to keep both a nearby flower and a distant mountain sharply focused at the same time, conventional optical microscopes face a similar challenge when imaging structures located at different depths inside the body. Tighter focusing of light improves spatial resolution, but at the same time reduces the depth range over which the image remains sharply focused.

item.title: How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle
item.description: A new topological model connects a centuries-old voting paradox to a surface with no distinct inside or outside. The post How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: 相比黑猩猩，人类为什么更容易患上骨关节炎？
item.description: 一项基因组学研究表明，人类关节软骨中关键缓冲成分硫酸化糖胺聚糖（sGAG）的含量仅为黑猩猩等类人猿的约三分之一。这种在演化过程中出现的基因表达下调与软骨成分改变，虽然塑造了人类独特的骨骼形态，但也可能使人类更容易患上骨关节炎等退行性骨骼疾病。

item.title: Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering
item.description: To invade red blood cells, the deadly protist creates a temporary molecular portal that disappears behind it — a door we can now see in fine detail. The post Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering first appeared on Quanta Magazine

item.title: 30万至10万年前，东亚大地上的古人类可能大多是丹尼索瓦人？
item.description: 许家窑人的身份在分子层面得到确认，也让研究者第一次有机会系统认识丹尼索瓦人的形态特征。

item.title: 对话许地生、张洁松：人机协作，如何攻克一个困扰数学界30年的猜想？
item.description: 最近，困扰数学界30余年的三维Ghys猜想，在中国数学家与AI协作下取得突破。

item.title: 在沃森追思会上，我重新认识Jim Watson
item.description: 9月28日，在沃森追思会结束后，我和博后老板Michael Wigler餐叙闲聊，期间他讲了一句让我印象很深的话：Double helix structure also made Watson（双螺旋结构亦塑造了沃森）。

item.title: 商周新书：《巴斯德传》 ｜ 周忠和作序
item.description: 商周撰写的科学三巨人传记，孟德尔与詹纳都可以被同时冠以科学家与博物学家的头衔，而巴斯德稍有不同，更像一位真正现代意义上的科学家。

item.title: 会“隐身”的纹身来了
item.description: 美国科学家开发出一种名为 PhotoTat 的智能纹身墨水，只需经过几秒钟紫外光照射，原本隐形的图案便会迅速显现，并可以在需要时再次“消失”。

item.title: 丘成桐谈AI与数学：这是最令人兴奋、也是最危险的时代
item.description: 10月11日，“丘成桐数学与人工智能实验室联盟”在北京宣布成立。
